There is a cruel twist inside this. The people who are best at the discipline are the ones with the least time to run it. A solo advisor said it better than any framework I have read: If you are working, you are not selling, and if you are selling, you are not working.

So here is the question I kept circling. If the rainmaker’s edge is a discipline and not a personality, can you turn it into a system that a whole firm runs?

I think you can. Not a personality you hire for, but an engine anyone in the firm can operate: Every key account gets watched, every key person inside it gets watched, and when something changes, whoever owns that relationship gets both the reason to reach out and the thing worth saying.

What that engine is really for became clear in one conversation. A principal wins the large majority of the engagements he actually gets in front of. His constraint is not closing. It is getting into more rooms, early enough to matter. The system is not there to replace him. It is there to get him more at-bats, earlier.

Zoom out, because the stakes are bigger than any one firm’s pipeline. There are tens of thousands of small expert firms, and right now they are squeezed from two sides at once. AI is eating the analyst work they used to bill for. And their growth engine, the rainmaker, does not scale and does not last. Going back to the room I opened with. Partners in their 70s and 80s. Revenue through two people. No way for anyone else to originate. That is not a rare firm. That is the shape of the whole category.

These firms have two futures. They grow past their rainmakers and outlive them. Or they die with them, or get absorbed by someone larger, because they never built a way to grow that did not depend on one or two people. That is the real choice in front of the category, and very few firms are making it on purpose.

The firms that make it through the next few years will not be the ones with the best analysis. Everyone will have that. It is already close to free. They will be the ones that took what their best rainmaker keeps in his head, knowing who matters and showing up at the right moment, and made it a system instead of a person. When analysis becomes cheap, relationship intelligence becomes one of the few durable advantages left. The firms best positioned for the next decade will be those that turn what their best rainmakers know into institutional memory that can outlast any one person.

articles.title: Decolonising economics means questioning where its ideas came from—and imagining new ones
articles.summary:
Economics shapes many aspects of our daily lives, from the prices we pay to the policies governments adopt. Yet many of the ideas taught as universal principles of economics emerged from a narrow historical context and have rarely been examined through a decolonial lens.

A recently published book, Decolonizing Economics, argues that economics is long overdue for decolonization. Its authors contend that the discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power shaped the development of modern economies and the economic theories used to explain them.

Decolonising economics means rethinking how we understand economic development and inequality. Rather than explaining prosperity through technology, markets and scientific progress, it examines how colonisation, resource extraction and exploited labour shaped today’s wealthy economies while contributing to underdevelopment elsewhere.

At its core, it’s about shifting away from an economy that benefits the elite to one that builds people’s capabilities.

As an economics professor, I’ve been restructuring my teaching based on my scholarship on critical microeconomics, critical macroeconomics and alternative ways to build the economy.

Questioning Eurocentric assumptions

Many foundational economic theories were developed by wealthy European men during periods of colonial expansion. Yet these ideas are often treated as universal principles rather than products of a particular historical context.

Eurocentric economic thought tends to position European economic development as the norm while presenting Indigenous and Global South economic systems as deviations. Decolonising economics challenges assumptions within mainstream theory about choice, rationality and economic value.

For example, the concept of scarcity emphasises that people must make choices because resources are limited. However, this can overlook how social and economic inequalities constrain choices. A bonded labourer may appear to have economic choices within a market framework, but coercion and exploitation mean those are not truly choices at all.

Decolonising economics also challenges the assumption that wages reflect an individual’s contribution or value. How can this assumption account for the historically undervalued labour of essential workers, women and other marginalised groups?

Similarly, research on poverty and decision-making challenges the idea that people always act as fully informed and rational economic beings. Psychological stress associated with poverty can reduce people’s ability to process information and make effective decisions. That stress can leave them more vulnerable to complex contracts, fine print and information overload.

Decolonising economics also calls for greater scrutiny of free trade theory, which has shaped global development policy. It was advanced by one of the wealthiest economists in history, David Ricardo. Yet many wealthy countries first industrialised through protectionist policies before promoting free trade abroad — a pattern one economist described as “kicking away the ladder.”

This kind of sustained critical examination of mainstream economic assumptions is central to the project of decolonising economics.

Recognising extractive economic systems

Decolonising economics also calls for examining how economic systems can reproduce inequality by marginalised communities in wealthy countries while relying on resource extraction and low-wage labour in the Global South.

Critics of the prison industrial complex, for example, argue that it generates profits while disproportionately affecting Indigenous and Black communities through higher rates of incarceration.

Hesquiaht author and business leader Carol Anne Hilton critiques the systemic economic exclusion and displacement of Indigenous people. She challenges the narrative that Indigenous people are a fiscal burden, arguing instead they are a source of economic strength. She also highlights how Canada’s prosperity is contingent on the extraction of Indigenous resources.

Globally, the economy remains structured around unequal exchanges, with the Global South providing resources and debt payments that exceed foreign aid received. The Democratic Republic of the Congo illustrates this contradiction: despite supplying much of the cobalt used in electric vehicle batteries, it remains economically disadvantaged.

Without addressing these inequalities, the transition to a low-carbon economy risks reproducing existing patterns of extraction.

Building alternative paradigms

If decolonising economics involves questioning dominant assumptions and recognising extractive systems, it also requires asking what economic thinking might look like beyond those frameworks.

This begins by expanding what counts as economic knowledge. Perspectives from the Global South, including dependency theory, as well as contributions from Muslim thinkers and other non-European scholars, offer alternative ways of understanding development, wealth and economic relationships.

These perspectives often emphasise economic approaches that value people, communities and ecosystems over economic productivity. They place greater value on social well-being, ecological sustainability and collective prosperity.

This approach informs policies such as economic reconciliation through greater Indigenous access to capital, resources and opportunities; climate justice measures that recognise unequal responsibility for environmental damage; and debt cancellation for debts incurred by governments without the consent of their people.

As journalist Nick Romeo has documented, alternative economic models already exist across the globe. They include true-cost pricing that reflects environmental and social impacts, job guarantee programs that address community needs and publicly owned digital platforms for gig work.

Others include worker co-operatives that narrow wage gaps between CEOs and workers, purpose-based companies that prioritise affordable housing and other social goals over profit maximisation, and participatory budgeting that gives citizens a direct role in public spending decisions.

Decolonising economics is a process that rests on challenging Eurocentric economic ideas, recognising systems of extraction, highlighting ideas from the Global South and building alternative models.

articles.title: Algorithmocracy: Of the algorithm, by the algorithm, for the algorithm
articles.summary:
For years we have heard that social media creates echo chambers because people within different social media networks consume divergent information. The most common theory as to why people are becoming more politically divided is that people are ignorant to the other side’s views because of the way algorithms section different people into different digital networks. Although this theory is the most widely accepted, it doesn’t adequately describe how social media platforms create public opinion today. The true form of postmodern divide is not that citizens do not see the same things. Instead, the same things are seen through wholly different algorithmic structures.

I have recently been reminded of this when discussing a political protest with a friend that gained significant coverage. We both did see the protest because we both watched the same marches, speeches, and many of the same protest related videos. Our conversation quickly turned to disbelief. Protest coverage on my feed was framing the movement as disruptive to civil order. The same coverage on my friend’s feed was framing the movement as protecting civil order. Again, we are not talking about different protests. We are discussing divergent viewpoints of the same protest.

This distinction is important. When most people talk about misinformation, they focus on the issue of the distribution of falsehoods or the absence of common facts. However, things have changed. The main issue is elsewhere. While most people focus on the event that attracted the most attention and the most outrage, Algorithms focus on the emotional and moral aspects of the event. The same Protest or Election or Court verdict or Policy Announcement can be different for different users and can be viewed through the lenses of entirely different meanings.

I am calling this new phenomenon Algorithmocracy. These algorithms do much more than recommend or suggest information. Algorithms actually govern public opinion. They don’t tell us what to think. In fact, they do the opposite. They tell us how to think, by surrounding us with certain information, emphasising certain facts, elevating certain reactions, and interpreting certain viewpoints. The real power of these systems is not how they control the information, but how they control how we think.

This model’s opposite of the typical “filter bubble” is built on collision rather than isolation. What social media platforms have learned is that there is nothing more engaging and thus more important to sustain user interest than national disputes and controversies. So, they make sure that every user is exposed to the controversies. Social media also knows that users more readily engage with content that aligns with their emotional state. Years of behavioural data of everything we have done and every subtle shift we have made such as pauses, comments, shares, likes and outages, give recommendation systems the ability to predict the best framing to engage us. This results in one user being presented content about law and order while another user is confronted with content about civil liberties. They both are covering the same subject but see a moral context that is specific to them.

The result of this is not just simple disagreement. Traditionally, when people are confronted with differing viewpoints, the response is usually along the lines of, “Oh, I didn’t know that.” But when two people talk about the same event but end up with opposing conclusions, the response is not fact vs. fact but moral vs. moral. It is assumed that the other person has witnessed what has been witnessed. From this, the response is to question the other person’s judgment, morality, intelligence, etc. This happens not because the facts are diverging but because facts are presented emotionally.

This architecture is largely commercial, but not ideological. Social media companies prioritise engagement, whereas presentations that are calm, balanced and nuanced do not encourage scrolling. Public outrage, certainty and moral urgency do. Therefore, algorithms will segment its user base and continuously show users interpretations of events that elicit the greatest emotional response. The goal, however, is not comprehension of events but the preservation of engagement (a.k.a. attention).

This is a relatively straightforward process. A large, nationally prominent event captures users’ attention. Within many users’ feeds, recommendations for the most popular interpretations will be prominently displayed. Users who do not agree will typically engage by posting comments, sharing the alternative views and/or verbally attacking the participants of the recommendations. The ultimate goal of the system is to sustain and encourage engagement.

This situation is extremely troubling for Liberal Democracy. Vigorous disagreement is the cornerstone of Liberal Democracy. In such a system, it is expected that citizens will disagree on value and policy issues, but will still have broad concordance on the events that are of public importance. Algorithmocracy shows that such a society can have shared events, videos and even prominent moments of public concern and still not share a concordance of public importance.

The consequences reach further than just politics. A minimum amount of shared reality is necessary for public trust, social unity, and the existence of legitimate institutions. Citizens begin to lose trust in each other and the existence of objective public debate as algorithms create a preference for maximising emotionally engaged interpretations in place of socially constructive interpretations. Each argument is simply another representation of the separate camps where supporting evidence is perceived to exist exclusively for each camp’s assertions.

Political theories have addressed the power and scope of politics and the issues of representation for centuries; the focus has historically been on who governs? In the context of the new digital reality, an equally valid question is who governs the representations of public life for the citizens? The power increasingly lies not with public representatives and institutions, editorial gatekeeping, or public service broadcasters, but with commercial enterprises focused on optimising profit over democracy, thinly disguised as social welfare.

Consequently, the greater challenge of the century is not the need for additional information or the addressing of misinformation. The architecture of attention and interpretation is equally fundamental for democracy. If we persist in viewing systems that determine information flows and audience engagement for maximum commercial profit as benign, neutral systems, the fault of citizen disengagement and of systems that strengthen and exacerbate polarisation will continue to be misplaced on citizens. The principal quandary of democratic systems now is not the fight for control of the information systems that dictate the narrative. Rather it is the fight for control over the systems that determine information engagement and audience interpretation.

-The Statesman (India)/ANN

articles.title: Exhibit review: In ‘Dialogue and Perception’, colour does all the talking
articles.summary:
Some exhibitions ask viewers to search for meaning. Others ask them to surrender to feeling first. Sagar Manandhar’s latest exhibition ‘Dialogue and Perception (Sambad ra Dristikon)’ belongs firmly to the latter.

Stepping into the Kala Salon, what strikes first is not the subject matter but the remarkable harmony of colour. Every painting appears to revolve around a dominant hue, allowing secondary colours to grow organically around it. The canvases are saturated with vivid blues, oranges, yellows and purples, yet they never descend into visual noise. Instead, the colours settle into an unexpected balance, creating works that feel energetic without becoming chaotic.

The exhibition is unmistakably abstract, but abstraction here never feels directionless. Strong geometric forms anchor each composition while carefully maintained lines provide structure beneath the apparent spontaneity. There is discipline behind every gesture. Thin borders often frame the compositions, suggesting restraint, yet somewhere within each work a section seems determined to escape those boundaries, pushing outward as though the painting itself refuses confinement.

Walking through the exhibit, one begins to recognise a distinct visual language. Certain rhythmic squiggles recur throughout the paintings, resembling sound frequencies frozen into colour. They weave across the canvas like vibrations made visible, hinting that the artist experiences the world less through objects than through resonance. Even the sequencing of the paintings within the gallery feels intentional, almost as if viewers are moving through different movements of a musical composition.

It is difficult to mistake these paintings for anyone else’s. Despite experimenting with new techniques and materials, Manandhar has developed a recognisable signature. His brushwork, layered acrylic lines and rhythmic mark-making create a consistency that ties the exhibition together while still allowing individual works to explore different emotional territories.

Texture plays an equally important role. Paint bubbles emerge from the surface, thick acrylic ridges catch the light, while scratched lines and raised forms introduce a physicality that photographs cannot fully capture. In many works, the surface itself becomes part of the narrative. The acrylic seems alive, refusing to remain a passive medium.

Manandhar reinforces this relationship with material through his process. Rather than treating paint as something secondary to the final image, he describes acrylic as carrying emotion in itself. He speaks less about controlling an outcome than about trusting the process, allowing meanings to reveal themselves as he works. His abstraction is therefore not an attempt to conceal meaning but to discover it.

That philosophy becomes evident throughout the exhibition. These paintings do not feel planned in the conventional sense. Instead, they resemble emotional snapshots—moments where feeling has been translated into colour before language has the chance to intervene. There is something strangely nostalgic about them. Although entirely abstract, many of the works evoke the sensation of childhood, when the world seemed impossibly bright and uncomplicated. They feel less like representations of memory than the emotions memory leaves behind.

His understanding of colour further distinguishes the exhibition. Manandhar repeatedly places complementary colours alongside one another—blue against orange, yellow against purple—allowing contrasts to generate unexpected harmony. Colours that conventionally appear incompatible somehow coexist effortlessly under his hand. Small droplets of paint occasionally interrupt otherwise cohesive surfaces, momentarily pulling attention away from the composition before eventually folding back into it. Even these interruptions seem deliberate, preventing the eye from settling too comfortably.

Gradients soften transitions between otherwise bold passages, while the combination of acrylic paint and marker creates subtle shifts in texture and line quality. One senses an artist continually testing what his chosen medium is capable of.

Perhaps the exhibition's most compelling idea lies in Manandhar's relationship with sound. He speaks of having a special connection with auditory experience, something that manifests visually through repeated rhythmic forms and textured surfaces. Different scratches and lines remind him of different sounds produced by various materials. His experiments extend beyond canvas altogether.

Recent works include acrylic sheets that are allowed to dry into independent surfaces, as well as glass engravings that resonate like singing bowls when struck. These material explorations challenge the expectation that painting must remain confined to stretched canvas.

Interestingly, Manandhar says he sees paintings through palettes rather than individual colours. Rather than asking what blue or red symbolises, he considers what an entire palette feels like. This perspective explains one of the exhibition’s most intriguing inversions. While red is traditionally associated with anger, passion or heat, Manandhar instinctively reaches for blue. Likewise, sadness or emotional heaviness often emerges through reds instead of blues. The emotional vocabulary is deliberately reversed, forcing viewers to question their own assumptions about colour symbolism.

His influences also reveal themselves subtly. Manandhar credits his father, veteran artist Kiran Manandhar, as his greatest inspiration, particularly admiring his discipline and enduring creative energy. He also speaks of his appreciation for Buddha Nepali’s illusionistic abstraction. Yet despite these influences, the work never feels derivative. It remains distinctly his own.

The exhibition is not without moments of unevenness. Some experiments, particularly the detached acrylic surfaces, still feel exploratory rather than fully resolved. Similarly, a handful of colour droplets appear visually disconnected from the surrounding compositions, momentarily interrupting rather than enriching the rhythm.

Yet these minor imperfections seem inseparable from the exhibition’s central philosophy of experimentation. Manandhar is clearly less interested in polished certainty than in discovering what paint can become.

There is a temptation when viewing abstract art to search immediately for familiar forms—a landscape, a face or a tree. Manandhar acknowledges this instinct himself, observing that people naturally cling to what they already recognise. His paintings gently resist that impulse. Instead of offering identifiable subjects, they invite viewers to experience movement, rhythm, texture and colour before interpretation.

By the end of the exhibition, the paintings begin to feel less like images than recordings. They capture fleeting emotional frequencies that exist somewhere between sound, colour and memory.

‘Dialogue and Perception’ is an apt title because neither exists independently in Manandhar's work. The conversation begins with paint and canvas, but it doesn't end there. It continues between colour and sound, artist and viewer, certainty and imagination. His paintings ask for neither agreement nor interpretation. They ask only that we look– and perhaps, if we stay long enough, learn to listen.

____________________________________

Dialogue And Perception (Sambad ra Dristikon)

Time: 11:00 am to 8:00 pm

Entry: Free

articles.title: Book review: The nurse who chose Jumla over the world
articles.summary:
Radha Paudel’s Madan Puraskar-winning ‘Attack on Khalanga’ has been out for 13 years now. The English translation itself, ‘Jumla: A Nurse's Story’, is coming up on a decade of being on the shelves.

The book recounts Paudel’s experiences leading up to, during and after the Maoist attack on Khalanga, Jumla’s district headquarters. It is a record of the poverty- and misery-filled lives of the everyday people of Jumla. There are striking examples of this misery in the book. For example, in one part, Paudel offers a bar of soap to a lady washing herself by the river. The lady begins to bleed from her hands after she uses the soap, her skin not used to it.

The book is also about the Nepali Civil War. Paudel shares such extensive details of the Maoist attack on Khalanga that one can picture what it might have been like.

But along with these two popular ideas about what the story is about, there is another increasingly relevant one—that of migration in the author’s case but also generally of immigration.

It is through listening to her father’s stories of Jumla when she was a child that Paudel grows curious about the place. He often used to tell her, she writes, that she should return to Jumla as an adult to do what she can to help the people of the district. Paudel herself grew up in poverty, but whenever she brought it up as a child, her father used to tell her that they may be poor, but poorer still were the people of Jumla.

The author does well for herself. After completing an undergraduate nursing degree, she goes on to get her master’s in public health. And when all of her friends from nursing school move to the cities and sometimes abroad, like to the United Kingdom, Paudel moves to Jumla.

She recalls with much disdain how her friends who have moved to the UK would call her up and tell her to join them. They would tell her about all the facilities and opportunities awaiting her there, only if she would move. Multiple times in the book, Paudel shares the sentiment that there is no lack of nurses in the UK; if she does not go, someone else definitely will. Where there is a lack is in Jumla, and there, no one is willing to go. This is her reason for going. Jumla needs her; the United Kingdom does not.

At times, it feels to Paudel that not going to Jumla would almost be immoral. It would be a betrayal of the people there, for whom her services could be and are the difference between life and death. Her retelling of the death of a pregnant woman in her arms, just days after she arrives in Jumla, is a particularly jarring one.

The question then asked of the reader is what their duty is and to whom their duty is. As someone with the ability to help, to not help is simply wrong action—the way Paudel sees it.

In the middle of a civil war, with increasing Maoist activity around Jumla, Paudel’s friends, her siblings, her mother and even her father, who had sown the seed of Jumla in her mind, all plead with her not to go. When the Maoist attack on Khalanga does come, and Paudel’s employers come to airlift her out of the district. She leaves, but as she does, she laments for the Jumlis who have no safe place to which to flee.

Paudel comes back to Khalanga four weeks after the attack. When writing her book in 2013, she was still actively working for the betterment of the people of Jumla. She wins awards and recognition for her work; she manages to raise tens of lakhs and help thousands of families.

It is difficult not to feel hypocritical or greedy when reading ‘Jumla: A Nurse’s Story’. Here is a woman of such drive and education and courage, someone who could create a comfortable life for herself no matter where she went and what she did.

But she chooses to live with the poor and the downtrodden, to eat and sleep and live like them and with them, even when she could very well end up dead. Throughout my read of the book, I was in awe of Paudel’s sheer selflessness and sense of duty. It very rarely felt like she did anything for herself.

She has unshakeable resolve and an ability to work through the darkness of doubt and uncertainty. And in the wake of life’s rat race, in the race to secure your passport and then your acceptance to a foreign university, then your visa and finally your ticket away from Nepal, Paudel’s book is a discomforting yet necessary read that asks the reader to think about what they should do with their lives and why.______________________

Jumla: A Nurse's Story

Author: Radha Paudel

Year: 2013 (in Nepali); English translation in 2017

Publisher: Nepalaya

articles.title: How Miss Nepal Cosmo 2026 Kashis Subba turned self-doubt into confidence
articles.summary:
Kashis Subba, 21, is a fashion model and stylist with a Diploma in Fashion Design. She has spent the last four years building her name in Nepal's fashion industry, earning titles such as ‘Face of Nepal 2023’ and ‘Model of the Year 2025’.

Crowned Miss Nepal Cosmo 2026, she now hopes to build an international career in fashion while inspiring young people to pursue their dreams fearlessly and grow into the best versions of themselves.

In this conversation with the Post’s Jony Nepal and Rivash Rijal, Subba talks about embracing vulnerability, preparing for Miss Nepal and using the platform to represent Nepal on the international stage.

What was the biggest inspiration in starting your pageant journey?

Growing up, I used to watch pageants. After joining modelling, fashion runways, and photoshoots, I had seen a lot of opportunities, and I really loved performing on stage. But I never thought I would be a pageant girl, because I always felt like a pageant girl needs really strong speaking skills.

That changed when I saw Miss Cosmo. I realised pageants are evolving. It is not only about speaking anymore; your performance and stage presence also matter. It gave me a vision that I could also do this, that I could create impactful change for my country and community through this platform.

Even so, I doubted myself. I'm only 21, without the strong academic or professional portfolio a lot of pageant contestants have. But this year, my mentor pushed me to join Miss Nepal. Even with four years of modelling experience and representing Nepal in Korea at 18, I always felt I still had so much to learn. My mentor told me: you'll grow, you'll gain clarity on your vision, you won't just grow mentally but be able to make a real impact on people. That convinced me to give the audition, even unprepared.

What was the preparation process like?

I worked incredibly hard. For 50 days, I only slept three to four hours a night. My two mentors pushed me constantly. There were moments of doubt. Thinking I was too young, that there were so many strong contestants, and that I could always try again next year. But my mentors reframed it as my winning mindset.

I told myself that even if I did not win, working on my weaknesses and turning them into strengths would matter for my life regardless of the outcome. I tried not to carry stress through the days. During training, we had fun, we teased each other, we played. Only at home in the evenings did the real work start.

What did it feel like when you won?

Before my name was even announced, I was mentally thanking everyone. My mentors, everyone who'd supported me. I thought of my grandmother, who passed away last year; my mentor always told me that when I feel nervous or afraid, to look up and remember she's blessing me.

That day, oddly, I felt calm and confident rather than nervous. I kept thinking, whatever happens, I was brought here to grow; this is a chapter of my destiny. When they said my name, I broke down crying. I don't remember much of the actual crowning—the crown, the sash—but I still feel that emotion vividly even now.

How do you navigate social media and public scrutiny now that you've won?

Winning this title comes with huge responsibility.

The whole country and the world are watching. No one is perfect, and I've never claimed to be. What I've always said is: I'm not perfect, but I'll keep working on my weaknesses.

I honestly have not had time to look at social media since winning. The people who watched me work—my team, the makeup artists, everyone at Hidden Treasure—they saw my effort and supported me. If criticism came from someone who actually knows me closely, it would affect me. But strangers judging a single moment who do not know the full story do not matter. Even in an imperfect moment, I showed courage by standing for myself. That is what I'm proud of.

What difference has the platform actually made?

I'm about to represent my country in Vietnam. The people there already show me so much love and support. Whether I'm competing, performing, or just introducing myself as Nepali, I feel like I'm making a real impact representing my country internationally.

What impact do you believe fashion has on your self-expression and identity?

Fashion has been part of me since childhood. I used to drape my mom's shawls and put on my own fashion shows at home, walking an imaginary ramp. One day I'd want to be a tomboy in baggy clothes, the next day I would want to be a Barbie. I have always liked being creative with my looks. I think that's just my personality.

What are your short-term and long-term goals?

No one in my family was in the fashion or glamour field, but somehow destiny kept drawing me here. To become a model, and now Miss Nepal.

I always wanted to serve my community and do good for my people, but I had not imagined it would be through this platform. Now that I have it, it feels like this is my purpose. Not just for myself, but for the people around me.

I have never been an academic person. Studying was never easy for me. But Miss Nepal demanded a different kind of discipline: photoshoots, runway work, working under pressure, sometimes until three or four in the morning, and I found I had endless energy for it. Preparing for this actually made me work harder than I ever did for school, and I realised that if I build a habit around something, it becomes easier.

I genuinely enjoy this work, and I believe it can create real impact. So my long-term goal is to keep going in this direction, even though the future is never fully certain.

articles.title: Two Nepalis killed on Romanian railway track
articles.summary:
Two Nepalis were killed after being hit by a train in Romania’s eastern city of Bacău early Sunday morning. Their identities have not yet been disclosed.

According to a statement from the Bacău Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (ISU), the two were struck by a train at around 3:21 am while walking along the railway line near Chimiei Street.

Emergency responders, including ambulances, rescue teams and medical personnel, reached the site shortly after receiving information about the incident. They found both individuals dead upon arrival, the ISU said.

Romanian police and railway authorities have launched an investigation into the accident.

“An investigation is underway to establish how they ended up on the railway line and the circumstances that led to the accident,” the ISU said in its statement.

articles.title: Australia tightens student visa rules, rejects 64 percent of Nepali applications
articles.summary:
Australia has rejected around 64 percent of offshore student visa applications from Nepal, marking the highest rejection rate recorded for Nepali applicants, according to official data.

The surge in visa refusals comes after the Australian government tightened its screening process for international students amid concerns over migration levels, housing pressures and the integrity of the education system.

Australia categorises countries under an “Evidence Level” risk framework to determine the level of scrutiny applied during visa processing. Education sector insiders say Nepal was recently moved to “Level 3”, the highest-risk category, from “Level 2” following a government review conducted several months ago.

The impact has been most severe in the vocational education and training (VET) sector, which traditionally attracts students seeking shorter and more affordable courses. Nearly 90 percent of Nepali applications for VET courses have been rejected, with only 56 of 549 applicants receiving visas, according to recent statistics.

Around 60,000 Nepali students are currently enrolled in Australian institutions. Of them, about 56,000 are existing students, while roughly 4,000 are new arrivals.

Data from Australia’s Department of Home Affairs shows a sharp decline in new student arrivals from Nepal. Between January and May this year, only 2,700 of 7,500 offshore applicants from Nepal were granted visas. During the same period last year, 7,167 of 8,028 applicants received approvals.

The uncertainty surrounding visa approvals, combined with rising application costs, has discouraged many prospective students. Applicants currently have to pay an application fee of A$2,500 (approximately Rs260,000), which is non-refundable even if the visa is rejected.

Sanjeev Pandey, a Sydney-based lawyer, said Australia had welcomed a large number of international students after the Covid-19 pandemic, but authorities later became concerned about patterns of students changing courses and extending their stay without completing their original programmes.

“The government may have also tightened student visa rules to address growing employment and housing pressures,” Pandey said.

The stricter visa regime has raised concerns among education consultancies and smaller institutions that rely heavily on international enrolments.

Khagendra Satyal, international business development manager at Central Australian College, said the decline in student arrivals had significantly affected the sector.

“Visas are now granted only after assessing what positive contributions an international student can make to Australia in the long run,” Satyal said. “Students applying from Nepal need to understand this shift.”

The immigration crackdown also comes amid growing political pressure in Australia over migration. Analysts say the rise of politicians with hardline positions on immigration, including Pauline Hanson, has contributed to a broader political push for tighter controls.

Lawyer Pandey said the tougher environment has affected not only prospective students but also those already in Australia. Renewing student visas, switching back to student visas after completing post-study work arrangements, and bringing spouses as dependants have all become more difficult, he said.

Obtaining permanent residency has also become significantly more challenging compared with previous years.

Despite the tightening measures, Nepal remains one of the largest sources of international students in Australia. Government data shows Nepali students account for around nine percent of Australia's international student population, making Nepal the third-largest source country.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: मर्चवारीमाईमा पूर्वाधारसँगै सामाजिक विकासमा जोड
articles.summary:
मर्चवारीमाई गाउँपालिकाले स्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा, कृषि, रोजगारी तथा सामाजिक विकासका कार्यक्रमलाई प्राथमिकताका साथ कार्यान्वयन गरेको जनाएको छ।

पालिकाले पूर्वाधार विकाससँगै सेवा प्रवाह र सुशासनलाई प्राथमिकतामा राखेर दीर्घकालीन योजनाका आधारमा बजेट तर्जुमा तथा कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गर्दै आएको छ। सडक, खानेपानी, सरसफाइ तथा अन्य भौतिक पूर्वाधारका साथै शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, कृषि, रोजगारी र सामाजिक सुरक्षाका कार्यक्रमलाई प्राथमिकता दिइएको पालिका अध्यक्ष गयाप्रसाद बरईले जानकारी दिए। स्थानीय सरकारको विकासलाई भौतिक संरचना निर्माणमा मात्र सीमित नगरी नागरिकको जीवनस्तर सुधारसँग जोडिएको बताए।'हाम्रो लक्ष्य सडक र भवन निर्माणमा मात्र सीमित छैन।

स्वस्थ, शिक्षित, आत्मनिर्भर र समृद्ध समाज निर्माणतर्फ केन्द्रित छ,'उनले भने। आधारभूत स्वास्थ्य सेवा, मातृ तथा शिशु स्वास्थ्य, सुरक्षित प्रसूति, नियमित खोप तथा पोषण एवं स्वास्थ्य सचेतनाका कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन भएका छन्। स्वास्थ्य संस्थाको भौतिक पूर्वाधार सुधार, औषधि तथा स्वास्थ्य सामग्रीको व्यवस्थापन, गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरीको स्वास्थ्य परीक्षण, बाल स्वास्थ्य परीक्षण तथा समुदायमा आधारित स्वास्थ्य कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिइएको गाउँपालिकाले जनाएको छ। कृषिलाई स्थानीय अर्थतन्त्रको आधार मानेर गाउँपालिकाले किसान लक्षित कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गरिरहेको छ। आधुनिक कृषि प्रविधि, उन्नत बीउबिजन, सिँचाइ, कृषि उपकरण, पशुपालन तथा व्यावसायिक खेतीलाई प्रोत्साहन गरिएको छ।

किसानको उत्पादन र आम्दानी बढाउने उद्देश्यले प्राविधिक सहयोग तथा विभिन्न कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गरिएको गाउँपालिकाले जनाएको छ। युवालाई स्थानीयस्तरमै रोजगारी तथा स्वरोजगारका अवसर सिर्जना गर्ने उद्देश्यले सीपमूलक तालिम, कृषि उद्यम, साना व्यवसाय तथा उद्यमशीलता विकासका कार्यक्रम अघि बढाइएको छ। प्रमुख प्रशासकीय अधिकृत उपमन्यू त्रिपाठीले सेवा प्रवाहलाई सरल, छिटो र पारदर्शी बनाउन प्रशासनिक प्रणालीलाई प्रविधिमैत्री बनाउँदै लगिएको बताए।

'स्थानीय सरकारप्रतिको नागरिकको विश्वास सेवा प्रवाहबाट स्थापित हुन्छ। त्यसैले सुशासन, पारदर्शिता र उत्तरदायित्वलाई प्राथमिकतामा राखेर नागरिकमैत्री प्रशासन निर्माणमा केन्द्रित भएका छौँ,'उनले भने। गाउँपालिकाले सार्वजनिक सुनुवाइ, सामाजिक परीक्षण, नियमित अनुगमन तथा सूचना प्रविधिको प्रयोगमार्फत सेवा प्रवाहलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाउने प्रयास गरेको जनाएको छ। उपाध्यक्ष आशा सिंहले महिला, दलित, विपन्न, ज्येष्ठ नागरिक, बालबालिका तथा पछाडि परेका समुदायलाई लक्षित गरी विभिन्न कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गरिएको बताए।

महिला सशक्तीकरण, सामाजिक सुरक्षा, शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य तथा सीप विकासका कार्यक्रमलाई वडा तहसम्म विस्तार गरिएको उनले जानकारी दिए। शिक्षातर्फ विद्यालयको भौतिक पूर्वाधार सुधार, शैक्षिक गुणस्तर वृद्धि, शिक्षकको क्षमता विकास तथा विद्यार्थीमैत्री वातावरण निर्माणलाई प्राथमिकता दिइएको छ। त्यसैगरी, खेलकुद, वातावरण संरक्षण, सरसफाइ तथा फोहोर व्यवस्थापनका कार्यक्रमलाई समेत गाउँपालिकाले अघि बढाएको जनाएको छ।

गाउँपालिकाका अनुसार विकास निर्माणका योजना छनोट गर्दा स्थानीय आवश्यकता र नागरिकको मागलाई आधार बनाउने गरिएको छ। योजना कार्यान्वयनमा जनसहभागिता, नियमित अनुगमन तथा पारदर्शितालाई प्राथमिकतामा राखिएको छ।

articles.title: अर्को दलले गर्‍यो भने सत्य पनि झूटो मान्छ!
articles.summary:
ढाँटछल केही छैन बहाना न्यून छन्

अभावमै हुर्किएर चाहना न्यून छन्

आफ्नै पेसा र कर्ममा व्यस्त भै

मनोरञ्जनका रमाना न्यून छन्।

अर्को दलले गर्‍यो भने सत्य पनि झूटो मान्छ

आफ्नो दलले गर्दाचाहिँ सबै गलत सत्य ठान्छ

राजनीतिज्ञ सबै नेता पिपलपाते जस्तो लाग्ने

मुख्य नेता मर्न गए दौडिएर त्यतै जान्छ।

हिउँको पीडा कति हुन्छ खगरलाई थाहा हुन्छ

पानीको पिर कति हुन्छ बगरलाई थाहा हुन्छ

मेरा पीडा बगर खगर दुईकै भन्दा बढी हुन्छन्

भोगिएका पीडाहरू सगरलाई थाहा हुन्छ।

खाने वस्तु पाए पनि खानुपर्छ घिच्नु हुन्न

आफैं कानुन बनाएर आफैं त्यसलाई मिच्नु हुन्न

गुण लगाउन नसके नि बैगुनबाट बच्नैपर्छ

जुत्ता बनी बोक्नेलाई टोपी बनी थिच्नु हुन्न।

सलाईको सोझो काँटी शिर जलेर मर्नुपर्छ

फलामको नि सोझै काँटी शिरमा ठक्कर खाने गर्छ

सोझाको शिर प्रयोग गरी नाफा लुट्छन् बाङ्गाहरू

सोझो मजदुर शिरकै भरमा बाङ्गालाई सेवा गर्छ।

नामर्द बाँच्छन् अर्काको आशले

कायर बचेका कर्मको त्रासले

सबैका बाँच्ने तरिका नै फरक

मर्दले बाँच्ने आफ्नै प्रयासले।

कहिले सुन्दर मुहारले तृप्त बनायौ

कहिले मीठो आहारले तृप्त बनायौ

अब म सदाका लागि तृप्त भैसकेँ

किनकि वचनको प्रहारले तृप्त बनायौ।

बालक वृद्धभन्दा पनि राम्रो रैछ बैँस

सबैलाई अझ राम्रो आराम अनि ऐस

यीभन्दा नि ठूलो के हो भनी सोध्ने भए

ढुक्कसँग भनिदिन्छु सबैलाई पैसा।

कसैलाई गर्व हुने गोरो छाला भएकोमा

कसैलाई ठूलो पेट र पुक्क गाला भएकोमा

सफलताको शिखर चढी कर्मवीर मान्छेहरू

गर्व गर्छन् शिरमा अबिर काँधमा माला भएकोमा।

जब मेरो जीवनमा उनको सवार भयो

केही समय जीवनमा बहार भयो

एक अर्काको खुसी खोसाखोस भएपछि

एकलाई अर्काको आँसु उपचार भयो।

articles.title: पूर्वअमेरिकी राष्ट्रपति बाइडेनको क्यान्सर फैलियो : छोराले सुनाए पीडादायी अवस्था
articles.summary:
पूर्वअमेरिकी राष्ट्रपति जो बाइडेनको प्रोस्टेट क्यान्सर शरीरका अन्य भागहरूमा फैलिएको छ।

सार्वजनिक मुद्दाहरूमा बोल्न जारी राखे पनि उनलाई पीडा भइरहेको छोरा हन्टरले एक अन्तर्वार्तामा बताएका हुन्। बीबीसी न्यूजसँगको अन्तर्वार्तामा हन्टर बुबाको अवस्थाबारे कुरा गर्दा भावुक भएका थिए। उनले यसलाई हेर्नु धेरै दुःखद भएको बताए।

‘क्यान्सर फैलिएको छ, उहाँको हड्डीमा मेटास्टेसाइज भएको छ र अझ अगाडि बढेको छ,’ उनले भने, ‘यो धेरै पीडादायी छ र यो धेरै हिसाबले कमजोर पार्ने छ।’ ८३ वर्षीय बाइडेन अमेरिकी राष्ट्रपतिको रूपमा सेवा गर्ने सबैभन्दा पाको उमेरका व्यक्ति थिए। उनको चार वर्षको कार्यकालमा उनको उमेर चिन्ताको विषय बनेको थियो।

आफ्ना उत्तराधिकारी राष्ट्रपति डोनाल्ड ट्रम्पसँगको बहसपछि पुन: चुनावको लागि आफ्नो दाबी त्याग्न बाध्य भएका थिए। त्यतिबेला उनले आफ्ना स्वास्थ्य समस्याहरू लुकाएको आरोपमा चर्को आलोचना सामना गर्नुपरेको थियो। पूर्वराष्ट्रपति बाइडेनले ह्वाइट हाउस छोडेको चार महिनाभन्दा कम समयपछि गत वर्षको मे महिनामा क्यान्सरबारे खुलासा गरेका थिए।

गत सेप्टेम्बरमा उनले छालाको क्यान्सरको लागि शल्यक्रिया पनि गराएका थिए। गत अक्टोबरमा उनले प्रोस्टेट क्यान्सरको लागि विकिरण थेरापीको एक चरण पूरा गरेका थिए।

मे महिनामा सीबीएस न्यूजसँगको अन्तर्वार्तामा पूर्वप्रथम महिला जिल बाइडेनले परिवारले रोगबारे थाहा पाउँदा स्तब्ध भएको बताएकी थिइन्। ‘साँच्चै भन्ने हो भने, मलाई रोग पत्ता लागेको याद छ, र यो साँच्चै स्तब्ध पार्ने थियो,’ उनले भनिन्। उनले यो पनि संकेत गरिन् कि ह्वाइट हाउसमा सेवा गर्दा क्यान्सर पत्ता लागेको थिएन।

‘ठीक छ, तपाईंलाई थाहा छ डाक्टरहरूले भनेका थिए कि, अमेरिकन युरोलोजिकल एसोसिएसनका अनुसार ७० वर्षभन्दा माथिका पुरुषहरूलाई अब पीएसए, रगत परीक्षणको आवश्यकता पर्दैन किनभने यो ढिलो बढ्ने क्यान्सर हो... मलाई लाग्छ कि ह्वाइट हाउसमा हाम्रो अद्भुत हेरचाह थियो, तर कुनै न कुनै रूपमा त्यो छुट्यो,’ उनले त्यतिबेला भनेकी थिइन्।

हन्टरले परिवारलाई यो गाह्रो भएको बताए। ‘यो हेर्नु साँच्चै दुःखद छ,’ उनले भने, ‘मेरो बुवाको बारेमा, अहिले उहाँको स्वास्थ्यको बारेमा म एउटै कुरा भन्न चाहन्छु, म चाहन्छु कि उहाँले अझ बढी गुनासो गर्नुस्, किनकि यो राम्रो छैन।’ तर हन्टरले उनका बुबा बाहिर नै रहने र उनका लागि महत्त्वपूर्ण मुद्दाहरूको बारेमा सार्वजनिक रूपमा बोल्ने बताए। ‘उहाँ अझै पनि आफ्नो काम गरिरहनुभएको छ,’ उनले भने, ‘उहाँ यो देशमा धेरै विश्वास गर्नुहुन्छ।’

मध्यावधि चुनावपछि पूर्वराष्ट्रपति बाइडेनले ‘प्रोमिस मी, अमेरिका’ नामक संस्मरण पुस्तक पनि प्रकाशित गर्दैछन्। एजेन्सी

articles.title: हर्क साम्पङ भन्छन् : बालेन जी भन्दा धेरै कूटनीतिक हुनुहुन्छ रवि जी
articles.summary:
श्रम संस्कृति पार्टीका अध्यक्ष एवं सांसद हर्क साम्पाङले प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह र राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टीका सभापति रवि लामिछानेबिच तुलनात्मक टिप्पणी गरेका छन्।

सामाजिक सञ्जाल फेसबुकमार्फत सांसद साम्पाङले बालेनभन्दा रवि धेरै कूटनीतिक छन् भन्दै दुवै बिच तुलनात्मक टिप्पणी गरेका हुन्। उनले शुक्रबारको संसदमा रवि छिरेर आफूसँग हात मिलाउँदै 'आज तपाईं बोल्दै हुनुहुन्छ भन्ने थाहा भएर म पनि आएँ' भनेर भनेको प्रसंग निकाले।

सोही प्रसंगकै क्रममा हर्कले बालेन र रविबिच तुलना गरे। उनले भने, 'हिजो रवि जी सदनमा छिरेर म सँग हात मिलाउँदै "आज तपाई‌ं बोल्दै हुनुहुन्छ भन्ने थाहा भएर म पनि आएँ" भन्नु भो। अर्थोक केही होला नहोला त्यो तपसिलमा राखौँ तर बालेन जी भन्दा धेरै कूटनीतिक हुनुहुन्छ रवि जी।'

articles.title: मर्चवारीमाईमा पूर्वाधारसँगै सामाजिक विकासमा जोड
articles.summary:
मर्चवारीमाई गाउँपालिकाले स्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा, कृषि, रोजगारी तथा सामाजिक विकासका कार्यक्रमलाई प्राथमिकताका साथ कार्यान्वयन गरेको जनाएको छ।

पालिकाले पूर्वाधार विकाससँगै सेवा प्रवाह र सुशासनलाई प्राथमिकतामा राखेर दीर्घकालीन योजनाका आधारमा बजेट तर्जुमा तथा कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गर्दै आएको छ। सडक, खानेपानी, सरसफाइ तथा अन्य भौतिक पूर्वाधारका साथै शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, कृषि, रोजगारी र सामाजिक सुरक्षाका कार्यक्रमलाई प्राथमिकता दिइएको पालिका अध्यक्ष गयाप्रसाद बरईले जानकारी दिए। स्थानीय सरकारको विकासलाई भौतिक संरचना निर्माणमा मात्र सीमित नगरी नागरिकको जीवनस्तर सुधारसँग जोडिएको बताए।'हाम्रो लक्ष्य सडक र भवन निर्माणमा मात्र सीमित छैन।

स्वस्थ, शिक्षित, आत्मनिर्भर र समृद्ध समाज निर्माणतर्फ केन्द्रित छ,'उनले भने। आधारभूत स्वास्थ्य सेवा, मातृ तथा शिशु स्वास्थ्य, सुरक्षित प्रसूति, नियमित खोप तथा पोषण एवं स्वास्थ्य सचेतनाका कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन भएका छन्। स्वास्थ्य संस्थाको भौतिक पूर्वाधार सुधार, औषधि तथा स्वास्थ्य सामग्रीको व्यवस्थापन, गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरीको स्वास्थ्य परीक्षण, बाल स्वास्थ्य परीक्षण तथा समुदायमा आधारित स्वास्थ्य कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिइएको गाउँपालिकाले जनाएको छ। कृषिलाई स्थानीय अर्थतन्त्रको आधार मानेर गाउँपालिकाले किसान लक्षित कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गरिरहेको छ। आधुनिक कृषि प्रविधि, उन्नत बीउबिजन, सिँचाइ, कृषि उपकरण, पशुपालन तथा व्यावसायिक खेतीलाई प्रोत्साहन गरिएको छ।

किसानको उत्पादन र आम्दानी बढाउने उद्देश्यले प्राविधिक सहयोग तथा विभिन्न कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गरिएको गाउँपालिकाले जनाएको छ। युवालाई स्थानीयस्तरमै रोजगारी तथा स्वरोजगारका अवसर सिर्जना गर्ने उद्देश्यले सीपमूलक तालिम, कृषि उद्यम, साना व्यवसाय तथा उद्यमशीलता विकासका कार्यक्रम अघि बढाइएको छ। प्रमुख प्रशासकीय अधिकृत उपमन्यू त्रिपाठीले सेवा प्रवाहलाई सरल, छिटो र पारदर्शी बनाउन प्रशासनिक प्रणालीलाई प्रविधिमैत्री बनाउँदै लगिएको बताए।

'स्थानीय सरकारप्रतिको नागरिकको विश्वास सेवा प्रवाहबाट स्थापित हुन्छ। त्यसैले सुशासन, पारदर्शिता र उत्तरदायित्वलाई प्राथमिकतामा राखेर नागरिकमैत्री प्रशासन निर्माणमा केन्द्रित भएका छौँ,'उनले भने। गाउँपालिकाले सार्वजनिक सुनुवाइ, सामाजिक परीक्षण, नियमित अनुगमन तथा सूचना प्रविधिको प्रयोगमार्फत सेवा प्रवाहलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाउने प्रयास गरेको जनाएको छ। उपाध्यक्ष आशा सिंहले महिला, दलित, विपन्न, ज्येष्ठ नागरिक, बालबालिका तथा पछाडि परेका समुदायलाई लक्षित गरी विभिन्न कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन गरिएको बताए।

महिला सशक्तीकरण, सामाजिक सुरक्षा, शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य तथा सीप विकासका कार्यक्रमलाई वडा तहसम्म विस्तार गरिएको उनले जानकारी दिए। शिक्षातर्फ विद्यालयको भौतिक पूर्वाधार सुधार, शैक्षिक गुणस्तर वृद्धि, शिक्षकको क्षमता विकास तथा विद्यार्थीमैत्री वातावरण निर्माणलाई प्राथमिकता दिइएको छ। त्यसैगरी, खेलकुद, वातावरण संरक्षण, सरसफाइ तथा फोहोर व्यवस्थापनका कार्यक्रमलाई समेत गाउँपालिकाले अघि बढाएको जनाएको छ।

गाउँपालिकाका अनुसार विकास निर्माणका योजना छनोट गर्दा स्थानीय आवश्यकता र नागरिकको मागलाई आधार बनाउने गरिएको छ। योजना कार्यान्वयनमा जनसहभागिता, नियमित अनुगमन तथा पारदर्शितालाई प्राथमिकतामा राखिएको छ।
